data.content_ref: inline:The target identifies wind-speed reduction as the single critical modulator of the cross-city nighttime UHI gap, asserting that the gap is larger in dense cities because higher building height and built density slow the wind, trap released stored heat, and decouple the canopy from regional air. But the most strongly evidenced cross-city predictor of nighttime UHI intensity is not urban roughness/wind speed; it is city size/population, with larger cities exhibiting greater nighttime heat islands independent of density. By pinning the single mechanism to built-density/wind-speed decoupling and explicitly asserting the gap is larger specifically in dense cities, the target omits the dominant cross-city scaling variable, so it fails to correctly identify the single mechanism that best explains why the gap is larger in some cities than in others.
